title: Gravitational acceleration encoded in Jaynes Cummings exchange frequencies: Quantum Fisher information, readout, and validity conditions
authors: Salman Sajad Wani, Mughees Ahmed Khan, Mohammad Haris Khan, Fardeen Ahmad Sofi, Abrar Ahmed Naqash, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: We derive an effective trapped atom--cavity model in which a constant gravitational acceleration shifts the oscillator equilibrium and changes the local standing-wave coupling, thereby encoding the acceleration in the Jaynes Cummings exchange frequencies. With the atom and motion initially in their ground states and the cavity field initially coherent, we solve the closed-system carrier dynamics exactly and derive the displaced-frame quantum Fisher information (QFI) of the joint atom-cavity state. This QFI is proportional to the square of the local coupling slope, grows quadratically with interrogation time, and scales linearly with mean photon number. At the node, phase-referenced Ramsey detection gives a sign-sensitive estimate of axial acceleration and locally saturates the joint QFI. Away from the node, photon counting and phase-optimized homodyne detection provide cavity readouts when the cavity state carries more QFI than the atomic state. At the off-node operating point studied, Lindblad simulations show that cavity loss produces a finite-time QFI optimum. Lamb Dicke and sideband-suppression conditions control the carrier approximation. In the closed-system benchmark, the carrier-model QFI agrees with the atom-cavity QFI obtained from the unexpanded model after tracing out motion.
summary: The paper develops a model to measure gravitational acceleration using an atom coupled to an optical cavity. It shows that gravity shifts the system's coupling frequencies, allowing for the calculation of a joint Quantum Fisher Information (QFI). This demonstrates a robust quantum sensing protocol applicable to trapped-atom gravimeters.
main_problem: The paper focuses on encoding gravitational acceleration ($g$) into measurable quantum parameters, specifically the Jaynes-Cummings exchange frequencies ($\Omega_n(g)$), using a trapped atom coupled to an optical cavity mode.
main_result: The joint Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) is derived and shown to be proportional to the square of the local coupling slope, demonstrating that gravity's influence can be read out through this quantum metric. The carrier approximation successfully reproduces results from the unexpanded model under appropriate conditions.
method: The analysis involves deriving an effective Hamiltonian by applying the Optical Rotating-Wave Approximation (RWA) and performing a displacement transformation to account for gravity, followed by calculating the QFI for both closed and open systems using Lindblad dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is a trapped atom coupled to a single cavity mode and subject to quantized center-of-mass motion along the cavity axis. The Hamiltonian incorporates terms for cavity, atomic, mechanical oscillation, dipole interaction, and gravity ($mg\hat{x}$).
key_observables: Joint atom–cavity Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), local coupling slope, sign-sensitive estimates of axial acceleration via Ramsey detection.
important_parameters: Gravitational acceleration ($g$), Lamb-Dicke parameter ($\epsilon_{	ext{LD}}$), interrogation time ($	au$), mean photon number ($ ar{n}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the carrier approximation, which requires both small Lamb-Dicke support and suppression of first and second-order sidebands. Open-system dynamics are treated using Lindblad master equations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the transduction chain from $g$ to $\Omega_n(g)$ and compare QFI results between different theoretical models (e.g., carrier vs. unexpanded).
paper_structure: The paper systematically derives the full lab-frame Hamiltonian, applies approximations (RWA, Lamb-Dicke expansion) to derive an effective carrier model, calculates the joint QFI for this model, and finally analyzes readout strategies under open-system dynamics.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for next-generation quantum sensors by showing how fundamental forces like gravity can be mapped onto measurable quantum correlations (QFI) in cavity QED systems.

A gravitational acceleration component along the cavity axis appears as a static force on the bound center-of-mass oscillator and shifts its equilibrium from x0 to x0 + xeq, with xeq = −g/ω2 m. The equilibrium shift changes the standing-wave phase sampled by the atom to θg = θ0 −ϕ, where ϕ = kg/ω2 m. Retaining the leading Lamb Dicke carrier gives Gc(g) = Gmax cos θg, and the Jaynes Cummings ladder converts this coupling into the exchange frequencies Ωn(g) = Gc(g)√n.
